canonicalExplanation.summary: Three sequence containers cover most needs. **`std::array<T, N>`** has a **fixed size known at compile time**, lives inline (no heap) and never grows. **`std::vector<T>`** is a **growable** array: elements are contiguous, indexing is fast, and appending is cheap on average, but when it runs out of **capacity** it **reallocates**, moving every element and **invalidating** all pointers, references and iterators into it. **`std::string`** is a vector-like container specialised for text. Use `reserve(n)` when you know the size in advance: while size stays within capacity, appends don't reallocate. Use `.at(i)` when you want **bounds checking**; `[i]` doesn't check.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner keeps a reference to the best score (`int& best = scores[0];`), then appends more scores. After enough appends, best points at freed memory and prints garbage. A vector stores scores for fast indexed traversal and reserves known capacity before retaining references during append operations. In this lesson you'll select and implement with string, array or vector for a stated ownership and size requirement.

examples.title: Scores in a reserved vector
examples.situation: A vector stores scores for fast indexed traversal and reserves known capacity before retaining references during append operations.
walkthrough: **A vector stores scores for fast indexed traversal:** scores[i] is a direct index into contiguous memory.
**Reserves known capacity:** scores.reserve(100) before any appends.
**Before retaining references during append operations:** first stays valid through 50 more push_backs, because size never exceeds capacity.
examples.result: The reference stays correct, and appends never reallocate.

examples.title: The week that grew
examples.situation: A learner stores 7 daily values in a vector and accidentally push_backs an eighth, which goes unnoticed.
walkthrough: The count is fixed by meaning: 7 days.
std::array<int, 7> can't grow, so the mistake can't compile.
Use .at(i) when the index comes from input.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: All standard sequence containers support the same iterator stability and random-access operations.
misconceptions.correction: They differ: array never reallocates, vector and string reallocate when they grow past capacity (invalidating references), and list/deque have other guarantees. Choose by the guarantees you need.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did the reference to scores[0] break?

analogy.example: std::array is **a 7-slot pill organiser**: fixed, never grows. std::vector is **a row of seats that moves to a bigger room when it fills up**: everyone moves, so a note saying "seat 3 in room A" is now wrong. reserve() is **booking the big room upfront**.
limitations: Real audiences notice moving; references don't.
std::string is the same row of seats, for letters.

steps.explanation: The vector reserves known capacity before appending.
A reference is retained to an element in contiguous storage.
Appends within capacity don't reallocate, so the reference stays valid.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing capacity and references. Step 1, Reserve: size is 1; capacity is 100. The vector reserves known capacity before appending. Step 2, Refer: first is &scores[0]. A reference is retained to an element in contiguous storage. Step 3, Append: size is 51; reallocated is no; first is valid, 72. Appends within capacity don't reallocate, so the reference stays valid.

recap.summary: To choose sequence containers, use std::array for sizes fixed at compile time, std::vector for growing collections (reserving when the size is known), and std::string for text, remembering growth past capacity reallocates and invalidates references, and at() gives bounds-checked access.
